title: Shared Circuits for Shared Grammar: Tracing Subject-Verb Agreement Across Languages
abstract: arXiv:2608.18545v1 Announce Type: new  Abstract: Multilingual large language models often generalize across languages, and prior work suggests that their internal mechanisms can overlap cross-lingually. It remains unclear, however, when such sharing emerges and whether it varies with the overt realization of the same grammatical operation. We investigate this question for present-tense subject-verb agreement, a morphosyntactic process that varies substantially across languages and is only weakly expressed in English. Using activation patching and attention analysis across 29 languages and five open-source model families, we identify the attention heads causally implicated in agreement and compare these head-level signatures across languages. We find that languages with overt person/number inflection exhibit more similar agreement circuitry than non-conjugating languages, with the strongest sharing appearing when the analysis isolates recovery of the inflectional contrast itself. translated_title: 共享电路与共享语法：跨语言追踪主谓一致
translated_abstract: arXiv:2608.18545v1 公告类型：新 摘要：多语言大语言模型通常能跨语言泛化，先前研究表明其内部机制可能具有跨语言重叠性。然而，这种共享何时出现以及是否随同一语法操作的表层实现方式而变化，仍不清楚。我们针对现在时主谓一致这一跨语言差异显著且英语中表达较弱的形态句法过程进行了研究。通过激活修补和注意力分析，覆盖29种语言和五个开源模型家族，我们识别了因果参与一致性处理的注意力头，并比较了跨语言的头部级特征。我们发现，具有显性人称/数屈折的语言比非屈折语言表现出更相似的一致性电路，当分析聚焦于屈折对比本身的恢复时，共享性最强。英语...
tldr: 本研究通过跨29种语言的分析发现，具有显性人称/数屈折的语言在主语-动词一致性处理中共享更相似的神经电路，且这种共享在恢复屈折对比时最为显著。
en_tdlr: This study reveals that languages with overt person/number inflection share more similar neural circuits for subject-verb agreement processing, with the strongest sharing when recovering inflectional contrasts.
